en: The Jātaka of the Fortieth Fifty:
The Chapter on the Tesakuṇa Birds
1. The Tesakuṇa Jātaka.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
“I ask you about Vessantara.”
"O bird, may it be well with you!
What excellent deed must be performed by one who desires to exercise sovereignty?"
“After such a long time, indeed,
my father Kaṁsa, the conqueror of Bārāṇasī,
having become heedless, [will encounter] me who am heedful.”
The father exhorted his son:
"By the very first [thought],
one should ward off false anger and laughter."
Then one should perform the duties;
that indeed they call the vow of a kshatriya.
Whatever ascetic practice you perform, my dear—
One should not again do that which, out of passion or hatred, one might have done previously as a result of doubt.
When a kshatriya ruler of the realm becomes negligent,
all his wealth perishes.
"O King, that is called misfortune.
When asked, both Śrī and Alakṣmī replied thus:
I delight in one who exerts effort,
who is energetic, and free from envy;
not in one who is envious and hard-hearted.
A man who is evil in his actions, O Great King,
finds delight in the ill-omened Cakkabhañjanī.
Therefore, being well-disposed toward all,
may you be a protector of all;
dispel misfortune, O Great King.
One should enter into existence with discernment.
For that man who is endowed with discernment and wisdom is indeed noble.
O Lord of Kāsi, he cuts off both the root and the summit of his enemies;
for even Sakka, the lord of beings, [does so].
One does not neglect exertion;
having established firm resolve in what is wholesome,
one sets the mind upon exertion.
Gandhabbas, fathers, and gods become companions to such a one who exerts himself and is heedful.
The deities attend upon him. Therefore,
my dear, being diligent and free from anger, perform your duties.
Exert yourself in your duties;
one who is lazy finds no happiness.
Right there are your steps of conduct.
This is the instruction:
it is sufficient to bring happiness to friends and suffering to enemies.
“O Kuṇḍalinī, you who consider yourself a kinswoman of the Khattiyas,
can you [endure this] while desiring to exercise sovereignty?”
"What indeed is the best deed that has been done?
"Two things, dear father,
are those upon which everything is established:"
The gaining of what has not been gained,
and the preservation of what has been gained—
know these, my dear, as the duties of ministers.
To one who is steadfast, skilled in the goal,
not prone to boasting, dear son,
sober, and not wasteful.
And whoever, dear son, would protect you and whatever wealth you may have,
he should guard it as a charioteer guards his chariot.
Thus he should have his duties performed;
having well-gathered his people and personally overseen his wealth, he should act.
One should not entrust one's savings or debts to another;
one should know for oneself one's own income and expenditure.
One should know for oneself what has been done and what remains undone;
one should restrain those worthy of restraint and encourage those worthy of encouragement.
Instruct the people regarding their own welfare,
O bull among charioteers;
let not those who are unrighteous be appointed by you.
They destroyed both wealth and the kingdom.
Do not perform actions, nor cause them to be performed, with haste.
For one who acts impulsively,
the dull-witted person later regrets it;
do not let him transgress against you by releasing his anger.
Severely provoked and excessively incensed;
for through anger, many families that were once prosperous have fallen into ruin.
"O dear one, do not act for the sake of harm,
thinking 'I am the lord' over women and men."
Let there be no sorrow for you,
O King who follows after sensual pleasures, though you have cast off the bristling of the hair on your body.
All enjoyments perish;
that, O King, is called misfortune.
Right there, those steps of conduct—
This is the instruction:
now, let the one who performs merit for the capable person be sober and not destructive.
“The virtuous one, O Great King, is [reborn in heaven],
while the immoral one goes to ruin.
We questioned the one of the Kosiya clan.
And likewise Kuṇḍalinī;
now you, Jambuka, declare which among these is the supreme strength.”
“There are five kinds of strength in the world found in a man of great stature:
therein, what is called the strength of the arms,”
The last is called strength.
And the strength of wealth, O Long-lived One,
is called the second strength.
And the power of ministers, Dīghāvu—
this is called the third power.
And the power of noble birth...
That is the fourth, without doubt;
and all these that the wise man attains.
Of all strengths, that strength is the best;
the strength of wisdom is the supreme strength.
One who is fortified by the strength of wisdom—
The wise person finds true welfare;
even if a fool should obtain the most excellent and prosperous earth, [he does not].
Whether by force or against his will,
another person acts toward him;
even if he is of noble birth, [he is still subject to this].
Having obtained the kingdom,
a kshatriya who is indeed lacking in wisdom,
O Lord of Kāsi, does not live by means of it at all.
Wisdom alone discerns what has been heard;
wisdom increases one's reputation and fame;
a person endowed with wisdom in this world—
Even in suffering, one finds pleasures;
yet no one attains wisdom who lacks the desire to hear it.
Without resorting to one who is learned,
who stands firm in the Dhamma and analyzes it,
one who knows the analysis of the Dhamma—
Rising at the proper time and free from indolence,
one who applies oneself at the right moment finds that the fruit of their action succeeds.
For one who does not practice the proper bases of conduct, who does not frequent the proper bases, and who does not act with a sense of disenchantment, [there is no liberation].
Right purpose ripens for one who is devoted internally and likewise frequents the sense bases.
For one who does not become disenchanted, the true goal ripens;
that which is designated as the application of yoga—
And the guarding of what has been gathered—
these, my dear, you should practice;
do not let yourself be overcome by idleness.
For through his own actions, the foolish man sinks down like a reed-hut.
"Practice the Dhamma, O Great King."
O Kshatriya, toward your mother and father;
having practiced the Dharma here,
O King, you shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
toward your children and wives, O Kshatriya;
having practiced the Dhamma here in this world, [you will attain happiness after death].
O King, you shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
toward your friends and ministers, O Kshatriya.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King.
Regarding vehicles and armies:
having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
in villages and in market towns;
…pe…
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
throughout the kingdoms and the provinces...
[etc.]
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
toward recluses and brahmins;
…pe…
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King,
among the beasts and birds, O Kshatriya;
having practiced the Dhamma here in this world, [you will find happiness after death].
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King;
the Dhamma, when practiced, brings happiness.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King.
The Sainda gods, together with Brahmā,
attained heaven through their well-performed deeds;
O King, do not be negligent regarding the Dhamma.
In that very place lie those steps;
this indeed is the instruction:
to associate with the wise is auspicious.
"Equanimity is the peace known by the wise.
Thus ends the first *Tesaṅkuṇa Jātaka*.
